summary: 1. High-stayed hooks (52–60%) jump straight into an immediate counter-intuitive statement or a second-person scenario in the first sentence without introductory fluff. 2. Low-stayed hooks (24–36%) fail by using passive background context or broad multi-clause setups before getting to the main point. 3. Top-performing titles pair recognizable real-world objects (cars, T. rex, eyes) with concrete numbers or questions rather than generic scientific discoveries. 4. Visual scale and immediate real-world comparisons (e.g., 'stacked like three small cars', 'no bigger than a small dog') drive view retention over abstract descriptions. 5. Shorter, punchier opening sentences under 12 words correlate directly with stayed_pct above 50%.
winning_hooks: State an immediate counter-intuitive safety/physics rule in sentence one (e.g., 'A car that folds up in a crash keeps you safer than one that doesn't.').
Use second-person present tense with direct sensory stakes (e.g., 'Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.').
Bust a popular myth in under ten words (e.g., 'The real T. rex probably couldn't run. Not even a jog.').
avoid: Contextual preamble and setup sentences before reaching the payload (e.g., 'Pluto seemed like our solar system's edge, yet astronomers...').
Generic introductory clauses that waste the first 2 seconds (e.g., 'Fossilized bones can last millions of years, but sometimes...').
Abstract institutional title framing like 'Why Scientists Missed...' instead of direct topic action.
next_experiment: Test direct second-person roleplay hook vs third-person statement hook on identical script topics (e.g., 'You are swallowing a cup of seawater every time you swim' vs 'Swimmers swallow an average of one cup of seawater per hour').
